summary:
Project details: SpotX

What it does: SpotX is a free, browser-based “blink comparator” for NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey. It lines up every SPHEREx visit to the same patch of sky on one grid, so anything that moved, brightened or faded stands out. Tombaugh used the same technique to find Pluto in 1930.

Planet X search: On the Planet X page you can follow Pluto, Neptune or Uranus through real SPHEREx frames. Each one lands where NASA JPL’s orbit predicts, within 0.3 pixels for Uranus and 0.8 for Neptune. The planet search then shifts and stacks 46 images along possible paths, which reveals a planet too faint for any single image. Without being told where to look, it found Pluto at 45 times the noise. A simulated test planet, planted in the real frames, was recovered down to 45 times fainter than Pluto.

Explore any object:

Step through visits as a sequence, blink, side by side, swipe, difference, or a red-green-blue “colour-time” view, where moving objects leave a rainbow trail.
Click a spot to see its spectrum across SPHEREx’s 102 colours. Molecules such as water and methane are labelled only when the data shows them clearly (3σ), with the paper behind each label cited.
Gaia and WISE markers show where known stars should be on each date, and SkyBoT flags known asteroids, so an unexplained mover becomes a “candidate for review”.
details:
Project details: SpotX

What it does: SpotX is a free, browser-based “blink comparator” for NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey. It lines up every SPHEREx visit to the same patch of sky on one grid, so anything that moved, brightened or faded stands out. Tombaugh used the same technique to find Pluto in 1930.

Planet X search: On the Planet X page you can follow Pluto, Neptune or Uranus through real SPHEREx frames. Each one lands where NASA JPL’s orbit predicts, within 0.3 pixels for Uranus and 0.8 for Neptune. The planet search then shifts and stacks 46 images along possible paths, which reveals a planet too faint for any single image. Without being told where to look, it found Pluto at 45 times the noise. A simulated test planet, planted in the real frames, was recovered down to 45 times fainter than Pluto.

Explore any object:

  • Step through visits as a sequence, blink, side by side, swipe, difference, or a red-green-blue “colour-time” view, where moving objects leave a rainbow trail.
  • Click a spot to see its spectrum across SPHEREx’s 102 colours. Molecules such as water and methane are labelled only when the data shows them clearly (3σ), with the paper behind each label cited.
  • Gaia and WISE markers show where known stars should be on each date, and SkyBoT flags known asteroids, so an unexplained mover becomes a “candidate for review”.

How we built it: A Python FastAPI backend (astropy, astroquery, reproject) and a static web front end. Images come straight from NASA/IPAC IRSA and planet positions from JPL Horizons. A pre-built snapshot lets the public site run on Netlify with no server.

Who benefits: Students, teachers and citizen scientists: the 2.7 million Zooniverse volunteers and the 125,000+ who have hunted planets on Backyard Worlds. There’s nothing to install and no account, and links can be shared.

Honesty: We make no discovery claims; the test planet is simulated to prove the method. Overlapping light from a neighbouring star is fitted out rather than hidden.

Next: Scan the whole sky automatically for moving objects nobody can explain, and let volunteers flag the best ones for professionals.

The 125K+ Backyard Worlds figure comes from an undated source; check it before you submit.
